1.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **14** or fourteen, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [And in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. It becomes clear in the next verse, understood in light of 37:8, that there were some significant cities that Sennacherib had not yet captured. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he captured one after another] or [and he captured many of them]

2.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֣וּר אֶת־רַב־שָׁקֵ֨ה מִ⁠לָּכִ֧ישׁ יְרוּשָׁלְַ֛מָ⁠ה אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֥לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּ⁠חֵ֣יל כָּבֵ֑ד
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **heavy army** with the information about the official whom the Assyrian king sent, and the information that he sent Rabshakeh **to Jerusalem** with the information that he sent him **from Lachish**. Alternate translation: [And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh with a heavy army from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah]

The term **Rabshakeh** is an Assyrian word, a title of an important official, that the biblical author is using in his account and spelling the way it sounds in his language. You could do the same thing, or you could translate the meaning of the term into your language. If you use the Assyrian word, you could explain what it means in a footnote. Alternate translation: [his field commander]

3.q: אֶלְיָקִ֥ים בֶּן חִלְקִיָּ֖הוּ & וְ⁠שֶׁבְנָא֙ הַ⁠סֹּפֵ֔ר וְ⁠יוֹאָ֥ח בֶּן אָסָ֖ף
3.note: Isaiah is introducing Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation.

The implication is that the phrases **over the house**, **the scribe**, and **the recorder** describe the official positions that these three men held in Hezekiah’s government. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who was the palace administrator … the royal secretary … the royal recorder]
The words **Eliakim**, **Hilkiah**, **Shebna**, and **Joah** are the names of men.

4.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַ⁠מֶּ֤לֶךְ הַ⁠גָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַ⁠בִּטָּח֛וֹן הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ
4.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the multiple levels of quotation in verses 4–20. There are three levels of quotation in this verse. The author is quoting what **the Rabshakeh** said (level 1). The Rabshakeh tells Hezekiah’s officials what he wants them to say **to Hezekiah** (level 2). This includes a quotation from **the king of Assyria** (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

4.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַ⁠מֶּ֤לֶךְ הַ⁠גָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַ⁠בִּטָּח֛וֹן הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ
4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, starting in this verse. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh told them to tell Hezekiah that the great king, the king of Assyria, wanted to know what this trust was that he was trusting]

The implied “you” in the imperative **say** is plural here because the Rabshakeh is addressing all three of Hezekiah’s officials. So use the plural form here in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one in whom you can trust to protect you from us!]

The king of Assyria is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [What is this trust that you have] or [In whom are you trusting]

The word **you** is singular here because the king of Assyria (speaking through the Rabshakeh) is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verses 20 and 21 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

5.q: אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ אַךְ־דְּבַר־שְׂפָתַ֔יִם עֵצָ֥ה וּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֑ה עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
5.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that Hezekiah is only speaking a word of lips when he says that he has counsel and might for war. The king asks in whom Hezekiah is trusting, that Hezekiah rebels against the king of Assyria.]

There is a fourth level of quotation here, in addition to the three that a note describes in the previous verse. According to the interpretation that the ULT follows, the king of Assyria (level 3), whom Hezekiah’s officials are to quote (level 2), as the Rabshakeh tells them to do (level 1), is quoting what Hezekiah himself has said (level 4). If you have decided to mark levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for this level as well.

The king of Assyria is using **a word of lips** as a common expression of his culture to mean “mere talk.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah, you speak only empty words] or [It is mere talk when you say]

5.q: עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
5.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one you can trust to help you, that you should rebel against me]

6.q: הִנֵּ֣ה בָטַ֡חְתָּ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִסָּמֵ֥ךְ אִישׁ֙ עָלָ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠בָ֥א בְ⁠כַפּ֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠נְקָבָ֑⁠הּ כֵּ֚ן פַּרְעֹ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠כָֽל־הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֖ים עָלָֽי⁠ו
6.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that behold, Hezekiah is trusting in Egypt to help him, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff. If a man leans on it, it goes into his palm and pierces it. That is what Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is like for anyone who trusts in him]

The king of Assyria is using the term **Behold** to focus Hezekiah’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

6.q: בָטַ֡חְתָּ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם
6.note: The king of Assyria is speaking as if **Egypt** were actually a **broken reed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you believe that you can rely on Egypt, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff]

The king of Assyria is using the possessive form to describe a **staff** that consists of a **broken reed**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in this broken reed, Egypt, as a staff]

7.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
7.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form to challenge the claim that Hezekiah’s official might make that they are trusting in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And you should not say to me, ‘We trust in Yahweh our God,’ since he is the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘To the face of this altar in Jerusalem, you shall prostrate yourselves’!]

7.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
7.note: The second-level and third-level quotations that began in verse 4 conclude at the end of verse 6. There are two levels of quotation in this verse. The Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s official directly (level 1), and he quotes what the official might say and what Hezekiah has said (level 2). If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for the levels in this verse.

7.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֛י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֥חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ
7.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that Hezekiah should not tell him that you Judeans are trusting in Yahweh your God. After all, Hezekiah himself is the one who has removed the high places and altars and told the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they must prostrate themselves to the face of the altar in Jerusalem.]

The word **you** is singular in the first instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s official. The word **you** in the second instance and the word **yourselves** are plural because Hezekiah was addressing all of the Judeans. So use singular and plural forms respectively in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **We**, Hezekiah’s officials would mean themselves and their fellow Judeans but not the Rabshakeh, to whom they would be speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **Judah** and **Jerusalem** represent the people who live in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Judah and Jerusalem]
This is a Hebrew idiom meaning “Before” or “in the presence of.” Alternate translation: [In front of]

8.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤ה לְ⁠ךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥⁠תֶת לְ⁠ךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
8.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [And now, please invite Hezekiah to make a wager with my master, the king of Assyria. Tell him that I will give him 2,000 horses if he is able to put riders on them for himself]

This is the beginning of something that the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. He implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote to Hezekiah what he says. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah from me, ‘And now]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point such as the implications of what they were just saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation.

8.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤ה לְ⁠ךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥⁠תֶת לְ⁠ךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
8.note: The implied “you” in the imperative **wager** and the pronouns **you** and **yourself** are singular in each instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verse 9 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

9.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים וַ⁠תִּבְטַ֤ח לְ⁠ךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠רֶ֖כֶב וּ⁠לְ⁠פָרָשִֽׁים
9.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But ask him how he would turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master. Tell him I know that is why he is trusting for himself in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen]

9.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים
9.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But even then, you would not be able to turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master!]

9.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְטַנִּ֑ים
9.note: The Rabshakeh is using one part of a person, his **face**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But how would you turn back a captain of one of the least servants of my master] or [But how would you force a captain to retreat even if he was one of the least servants of my master]

The Rabshakeh is using the possessive form to describe a **captain** who would be **one of the least servants** of the king of Assyria, that is, one of his weakest soldiers. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a captain who was among the least servants of my master]

This is the end of what the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. In the next verse, the Rabshakeh quotes the end of the message from Sennacherib that he wants the officials to give to Hezekiah. If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate closing punctuation at the end of this verse.

10.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
10.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that the king of Assyria says that he has not come up against this land to destroy it without Yahweh. Yahweh told him to go up against this land and destroy it]

10.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ
10.note: This is the beginning of something that Sennacherib is saying directly to Hezekiah. It is the rest of the message that the Rabshakeh began to quote in verses 4–6. The Rabshakeh implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote this to Hezekiah as something that Sennacherib has said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says the great king, “And have I come up]

10.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֑⁠הּ
10.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not think that I have come up against this land to destroy it without Yahweh!]

Sennacherib is not using the phrase **without Yahweh** to mean that Hezekiah should not think that he has come without Yahweh accompanying him. Rather, he means that he has come after receiving a command from Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [without receiving a command to do so from Yahweh]

11.note: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your servants,]

11.q: דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ
11.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since we, your servants, understand Aramaic, please speak to us in that language]

Eliakim is using the name of the dialect of Hebrew, **Judean**, that people spoke in the kingdom of Judah. Some versions use the name of the language rather than the name of this dialect and say “in Hebrew.” If you have decided to use the same names in your translation that the biblical author does, you may wish to use the name, **Judean**, here. If not, you may wish to use the name “Hebrew” here.

Here, **ears** represent “hearing.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the hearing of the people who are on the wall] or [, since the people who are on the wall can hear us]

12.q: הַ⁠אֶ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣⁠נִי אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה הֲ⁠לֹ֣א עַל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַ⁠יֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣⁠חוֹמָ֔ה לֶ⁠אֱכֹ֣ל אֶת־חראי⁠הם וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־שיני⁠הם עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
12.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My master did not send me to speak these words only to your master and to you! He also sent me to speak them to the men sitting on the wall, who will eat their dung and drink their urine with you!]

Rabshakeh is using the term **words** to represent what his **master** said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this message]

Even though the author says that the Rabshakeh spoke to **them**, the word **your** and the word **you** in its first instance are singular because the Rabshakeh is replying directly to Eliakim, who spoke on behalf of all three Judean officials. The word **you** in its second instance is plural because the Rabshakeh is including Shebnah and Joah in what he says will happen. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

13.note: The author probably does not mean that the Rabshakeh had been sitting down and having a private conversation with the Judean officials and that he then **stood** up. If the conversation had been private, there would have been no need for Eliakim to ask him to speak in Aramaic so that the people on the wall would not understand. So the author probably means that the Rabshakeh stood in such a way that his speech to the people on the wall would seem even more forceful and intimidating. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh assumed a dominating stance]
See how you have translated the phrase **and said** elsewhere when it introduces a direct quotation.

14.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥א לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־יוּכַ֖ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם
14.note: See the note about the multiple levels of quotation in the introduction to this chapter. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah deceive you, since he is not able to deliver you]

14.q: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥א לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־יוּכַ֖ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם
14.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Hezekiah is not able to deliver you, do not let him deceive you]

The word **you** is plural in both of these instances because king of Assyria, speaking through the Rabshakeh, is addressing the Judeans who have gathered on the city wall. For the same reason, the word “you” and the implied “you” in imperatives are also plural throughout verses 15–17. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

15.q: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
15.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

15.q: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
15.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah make you trust in Yahweh by telling you that delivering, Yahweh will deliver all of you, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria]

According to the king of Assyria, Hezekiah has been repeating forms of the verb **deliver** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will certainly deliver us]
By **us**, Hezekiah means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction, here and in verse 32.

The expression **will not be given** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not give this city]
Here, **hand** represents “control” or “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the control of]

16.note: Rabshakeh is saying what he wants the people to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that you do not listen to Hezekiah] or [You should not listen to Hezekiah]

16.q: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤⁠י בְרָכָה֙ וּ⁠צְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
16.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [for the king of Assyria is telling you to make a blessing with him and come out to him. Then you will be able to eat, a man of his vine and a man of his fig tree, and drink, a man from the waters of his well]

Here, **a blessing**, meaning a gift, represents “a peace agreement,” since in this culture people exchanged gifts when they made peace agreements. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make a peace agreement with me]

16.q: וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
16.note: Rabshakeh is using **a man of his** vine and **a man of his** fig tree as a common expression of the culture to mean “each man may access his own.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let each of you eat from his vine and fig tree]

17.q: עַד־בֹּאִ֕⁠י וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֥י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם אֶ֤רֶץ דָּגָן֙ וְ⁠תִיר֔וֹשׁ אֶ֥רֶץ לֶ֖חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִֽים
17.note: There are three levels of quotation here. Isaiah is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

17.q: עַד־בֹּאִ֕⁠י וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֥י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם אֶ֤רֶץ דָּגָן֙ וְ⁠תִיר֔וֹשׁ אֶ֥רֶץ לֶ֖חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִֽים
17.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [until he comes and takes you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards]
Since the rest of the items on this list are agricultural products, these **vineyards** may represent the products of vineyards. Alternate translation: [and grapes]

18.q: הַ⁠הִצִּ֜ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֔⁠וֹ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
18.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [None of the gods of the nations actually delivered the land where people worshiped it from the hand of the king of Assyria!]

18.q: הַ⁠הִצִּ֜ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֔⁠וֹ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
18.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The Rabshakeh tells you to consider that none of the gods of the nations has delivered its land from the hand of the king of Assyria]

The Rabshakeh is using the term **a man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “any.” If this term does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Did any of the gods of the nations deliver his land]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of the king of Assyria, and similarly in the next two verses]

The king of Assyria is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a triumphant declaration. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [from my hand]

19.q: אַיֵּ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י חֲמָת֙ וְ⁠אַרְפָּ֔ד אַיֵּ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י סְפַרְוָ֑יִם & וְ⁠כִֽי־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
19.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [The gods of Hamath and Arpad did nothing to help those people! The gods of Sepharvaim did nothing to help those people! Indeed, the gods of Samaria did not deliver it from my hand!]

19.q: אַיֵּ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י חֲמָת֙ וְ⁠אַרְפָּ֔ד אַיֵּ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י סְפַרְוָ֑יִם & וְ⁠כִֽי־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
19.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The Rabshakeh points out that the gods of Hamath and Arpad did nothing to help those people, and the gods of Sepharvaim did nothing to help those people, and in fact the gods of Samaria did not deliver it from his hand]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to the gods that the king has just listed. It refers generally back to “the gods of the nations” in the previous verse and specifically to the gods that the people of the kingdom of Israel, called **Samaria** here, were worshiping. Alternate translation: [did the gods of Samaria deliver it]

20.q: מִ֗י בְּ⁠כָל־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָֽ⁠אֲרָצוֹת֙ הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠יָּדִ֑⁠י כִּֽי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
20.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form to emphasize that none of the gods of other nations have been able to rescue their lands from the Assyrian king. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You cannot name any of the gods of the lands that have delivered their land from my hand, so do not believe that Yahweh will deliver Jerusalem from my hand!]

20.q: מִ֗י בְּ⁠כָל־אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָֽ⁠אֲרָצוֹת֙ הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠יָּדִ֑⁠י כִּֽי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
20.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king emphasizes that none of the gods of the lands have delivered their lands from his hand, so you should not believe that Yahweh will deliver Jerusalem from his hand]

In this instance, the word **land** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the lands where these **gods** were worshiped. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “land.” Alternate translation: [their lands]

21.q: וַֽ⁠יַּחֲרִ֔ישׁוּ וְ⁠לֹֽא־עָנ֥וּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ דָּבָ֑ר כִּֽי־מִצְוַ֨ת הַ⁠מֶּ֥לֶךְ הִ֛יא לֵ⁠אמֹ֖ר לֹ֥א תַעֲנֻֽ⁠הוּ
21.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But since it was a commandment of the king, saying, “You shall not answer him,” the people were silent and did not answer him a word]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [But the people said nothing in response to him]

22.note: The expression **torn** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [tore their clothes and came to Hezekiah]
See how you indicated the symbolic significance of tearing one’s clothes earlier in this book.
